input.rationale: The marker question was the last account resting only on a reading, and the transfer-campaign receipt I filed measured exactly its subject, so this turn promotes it from source reasoning to a measured account. The mechanism is unchanged: the lease is evaluated as force := bytes.Equal(m.GetContext(), []byte(campaignTransfer)) on the inLease guard, so a higher-term MsgVote or MsgPreVote carrying that marker is not ignored - the receiver adopts the higher term and becomes a follower - whereas an ordinary request is dropped without a word. What the receipt adds is the observation on the receiving side: a transfer-marked vote request delivered to an incumbent leader serving inside its live lease was not suppressed at all, the incumbent adopted term 3 and became a follower, and its ballot was a rejection only because the candidate's advertised log was behind its own, which is the isUpToDate check rather than the lease. Two contrasts in the same family keep that from being an artefact: the same follower withheld an ordinary campaign's pre-vote under the same lease, and the earlier forged-election receipt records the marker-absent counterpart, where the incumbent answered neither the pre-vote nor the vote request at all. So the marker is precisely the difference between a request the lease discards and one it lets through, which is what this question asked, and I have moved the conclusion to violated so it matches the sibling measurement of the same predicate. The defect judgment does not move: the marker is a claim about the sender's own internal precondition, the receiver holds no record to check it against, and the snapshot assigns it no verification duty. I also verified the paired premise while I was here: the incumbent in the forged-election receipt really did answer neither request, so the account that the lease suppressed both there is accurate and needs no correction.

interpretations.rationale: The question is answered yes, and it is now answered by observation rather than only by reading. On the source side the mechanism is exact: the guard is written as force := bytes.Equal(m.GetContext(), []byte(campaignTransfer)) and the higher-term vote request is discarded only when force is false and inLease holds, so a request carrying the marker is not discarded at all - the receiver adopts the higher term and becomes a follower - while an ordinary request from the same peer is dropped silently, and the marker itself is produced only by campaign() when the campaign is a transfer. On the observation side, the sibling receipt delivers exactly such a request to an incumbent that was serving inside its live lease: the trigger produced two vote requests with transfer_context true (index 66 of CheckRun 026b6c86522d454299d1f3ca358c009e), the incumbent answered rather than ignoring (index 67, responded true), and it ended as a follower at the higher term (index 69, StateFollower at term 3 where its own admission event had recorded StateLeader at term 2). Its answer was a rejection rather than a grant, and the reason matters for reading the bypass correctly: the candidate advertised a last entry behind the incumbent's own, so isUpToDate refused the ballot even though the lease had let the request through - the lease is skipped, the log check is not. Two contrasts in the same family pin the difference to the marker. The same follower withheld an ordinary campaign's pre-vote under the same lease immediately before the trigger (index 65, granted false), and in the earlier forged-election receipt, where no marker is present, the incumbent answered neither the pre-vote nor the vote request at all (indices 12 and 16 of CheckRun ab6a2e0bcad44cc9beea9c847694939a). So the marker is the difference between a request the lease discards and one it lets through, which is what this question asked; That measurement is recorded with a violated conclusion on the sibling question, where the experiment that produced it is bound; this account stays explained because it carries no fixed experiment of its own, and the observation is cited here as corroboration of the mechanism the sources describe. The defect claim stays refuted for the reason recorded when the question was registered: the marker is a statement about the sender's own internal precondition, the receiver keeps no record of a pending transfer to compare it against, the context field is neither authenticated nor checked, and no statement in the snapshot places a verification duty on the receiver - so this is the same class of boundary as the term-less network message rather than a second instance of the missing filter.

knowledge.assertion: The lease is skipped when the incoming vote request carries the CampaignTransfer marker; the receipt shows that effect on the receiving side - the marked request was answered instead of dropped, the term advanced, and the receiver demoted, while the unmarked request in the same fixture was withheld entirely.

counterevidence: The bypass does not buy a ballot by itself: in the measured case the recipient skipped its lease and still rejected the vote on isUpToDate grounds (index 67 of the revised receipt), so what the marker removes is the lease delay, not the log check.

The behaviour is deliberate rather than accidental: campaign() attaches the marker precisely so that a leadership transfer is not blocked by the lease it is meant to override, and the receiving side is designed to trust the leader's instruction that produced it.

A node that campaigns normally never carries the marker, which the same family shows twice over: the ordinary pre-vote was withheld under the live lease (index 65), and in the marker-absent forged-election receipt the incumbent answered neither request at all (indices 12 and 16 of CheckRun ab6a2e0bcad44cc9beea9c847694939a).

Relying on the bypass requires a sender that claims an internal precondition it does not hold, which is outside the crash-fault model; a source statement placing a verification duty on the receiver would reopen the refutation, and none has been found in the snapshot.

interpretations.rationale: The current account rests on read source plus a native construction probe (not yet a retained receipt). MsgForgetLeader is generated only by the local ForgetLeader API, is never put on the wire by any code path in the snapshot, and stepFollower implements it as a local authority-state change (r.lead = None). The module's own inbound filter exists precisely to stop locally-generated types from being delivered from peers, but the type is missing from isLocalMsg, so RawNode.Step accepts it and, because its term field is absent (0), Step treats it as a local message and skips term checks; stepFollower then clears r.lead. With CheckQuorum+PreVote that removal of the leader context disables the lease test that otherwise suppresses support for a candidate whose log is already up to date, so an unauthenticated peer message converts the follower from 'silent' to 'grant' for the same pre-vote request. The retained suite does not contradict this: TestIsLocalMsg/TestIsResponseMsg enumerate every other MessageType but not MsgForgetLeader, and the interaction tests call RawNode.ForgetLeader directly, so neither covers the classification. Remaining scope limits: a single inbound message affects one node, the election still needs a quorum of grants, ReadOnlyLeaseBased refuses the change entirely (so lease-based reads are protected), and the next leader message restores r.lead. Registered gap: the length of that window and whether a quorum can be reached inside it. The requested experiment supplies the discriminating comparison set and its receipt must be read before the account is treated as execution-backed.
limitations: No retained receipt yet: the mechanism is established by source reading and by a native probe in a scratch copy whose output is not a controller receipt.

interpretations.rationale: The retained execution confirms the sourced suspicion. Comparison 2 (acceptance predicate) has a valid witness at index 4: a message of the type only the local ForgetLeader API produces, sent by peer 3 in wire form (From=3, To=2, no term field), is accepted by RawNode.Step with no error, and the follower's Lead drops from 1 to 0. Comparison 3 (consequence) has a valid witness at index 5: the same real MsgPreVote from an up-to-date candidate that produced no response while the lease held (control, comparison 1, holds at index 3) is answered with MsgPreVoteResp Reject=false once the leader context has been cleared. Comparison 0 holds at index 2, so the inbound filter itself works for a type that is classified local (MsgCheckQuorum from the same sender returns ErrStepLocalMsg and leaves Lead=1): the gap is specific to MsgForgetLeader's absence from isLocalMsg, which reading of util.go and the retained (equally incomplete) TestIsLocalMsg list already indicated. The mechanism is therefore a real authority/context-validity defect with bounded disruption impact: it defeats the intended 'a quorum must agree the leader is dead' condition that the ForgetLeader API documents, using a message the module's own inbound contract is supposed to reject. interpretations.rationale: The persistence question is answered yes, and the wiring revision is what made it answerable: each round now has its own admission event, so all six comparisons completed. Control: the round without a forged message granted nothing and produced no response at all (index 29), so withholding under the lease is real and not an artefact of the candidate. Persistence: the accepted message cleared the leader context and the identical retried pre-vote was granted in round 1 (index 32), round 2 (index 35) and round 3 (index 38) - three independent witnesses, each with its own admission event. Repair: the two comparisons that matter for attribution hold (indices 33 and 36), i.e. after each forgery the leader's real heartbeat restored lead from 0 to 1, so the repeated success of the forgery is the sender's cadence defeating a working repair rather than a broken repair path. Queueing happens only in stepLeader's MsgReadIndex arm when the leader has not yet committed in its own term (raft.go 1361-1368); completion happens only through releasePendingReadIndexMessages (raft.go 2127-2143), which guards on committedEntryInCurrentTerm and is invoked from exactly one place, the leader's append-response commit path (raft.go 1548-1556); and a search for the field shows no writer on any leadership-change path (raft.go 428-435 declares it, and no other occurrence exists). The caller contract in the same snapshot spells this out - read requests can be lost without notice and the application must retry - so the module neither violates a promise nor leaves a caller stranded who followed the documented contract. interpretations.rationale: The question is answered from the sources and the answer is a design fact rather than a defect. Each ordering violation an application could commit - rewriting committed entries, committing past the last index, applying out of order or past committed, or accepting application past committed - reaches a guard that panics, so the bookkeeping cannot be quietly advanced or rewound by a misreporting client; the two tolerated cases are treated differently on purpose (the outstanding-size counter saturates at zero, and further application pauses until the client acknowledges progress). interpretations.rationale: The question is answered yes on the mechanism and no on the defect, from sources only. The lease is written as force := bytes.Equal(m.GetContext(), []byte(campaignTransfer)) and the higher-term vote request is discarded only when force is false and inLease holds, so a sender that sets that context is answered: the receiver adopts the higher term, becomes a follower with r.lead = None, and then evaluates canVote, whose third clause (MsgPreVote with a term above the receiver's own) or its reset vote/leader state makes the grant available, subject to isUpToDate. The marker has exactly one producer in the snapshot: campaign() sets Context = []byte(campaignTransfer) when t == campaignTransfer, the campaign that begins in stepFollower's MsgTimeoutNow case via r.hup(campaignTransfer) and that increments the term and sends MsgVote at the new term. Two consequences follow and both matter for how the lease should be read. First, the bypass is narrow by construction: a node campaigning on its own, including a stale one that has lost contact with the leader, never carries the marker, which is why the lease still withheld the vote in every receipt of the main account. Second, the trust it places is in a statement about the sender rather than in anything the receiver holds: the receiving node keeps no record of a pending transfer and the context field is neither authenticated nor compared with local state, so it cannot tell a real transfer from a claimed one. That second point is what decides the judgment, and it is the same shape as the term-less network message this run already refuted: a sender claiming an internal precondition it does not hold is outside the crash-fault model the audit prioritises, and the snapshot states no duty for the receiver to verify a transfer it was told about. I therefore record the mechanism as a fact and the defect claim as refuted rather than asserted, with the empirical half left to the registered discriminator.

The behaviour is deliberate rather than accidental: campaign() attaches the marker precisely so that a leadership transfer is not blocked by the lease it is meant to override, and the receiving side is designed to trust the leader's instruction that produced it.

A node that campaigns normally never carries the marker, so the lease continues to protect the incumbent against ordinary election traffic, which is what every receipt of the main account shows by measurement.

interpretations.rationale: The question is answered from the sources and the answer is a design fact rather than a defect.
